title: Speech language features predict six-year Alzheimer dementia progression in a small cohort
summary: In 166 Framingham Heart Study participants with mild cognitive impairment, pretrained language embeddings of recorded cognitive-test transcripts supported retrospective prediction of progression to Alzheimer dementia within six years. Nested, participant-grouped cross-validation gave the text-only model an AUC of 0.778 and accuracy of 78.2%. The predominantly White, older cohort and lack of prospective external validation limit generalization; this is not a demonstrated screening or treatment benefit.
ai_technology: Universal Sentence Encoder; ensemble logistic regression

evidence.tested: Nested, stratified group cross-validation repeated three times on 166 participants:90 progressed and 76 remained MCI. Text-only AUC 0.778 compared with 0.713 for traditional neuropsychological test scores in this study.
evidence.unknown: No prospective clinical deployment, independent external cohort or patient-benefit trial. Outcomes include Alzheimer dementia with stroke or mixed vascular disease; results are not a pathology-specific diagnosis.
evidence.ai_role: Universal Sentence Encoder generated 512-dimensional transcript and subtest embeddings; feature selection and logistic-regression ensembles linked these semantic representations to subsequent dementia classifications.

source_review.scope: Exact primary article-front DOI/title/PMCID and date; full relevant model Methods, Results and limitations; fresh PubMed publication types and correction/retraction relationship metadata.
